sources.news_title: Dubai Step: Trump Declares 'Economic D-Day' on Iran
sources.text:
George W. Bush got the world's attention by drawing a line after 9/11. "You're either with us or against us," Bush warned when it came to radical Islamic terrorism. It provided a clarifying moment in American foreign policy, and carried enough of a military and economic threat that forced cooperation from unlikely sources.
This morning, Donald Trump played the same card Bush did, and against the same type of threat. Trump didn't use precisely the same formulation, but the point comes through clearly. Anyone doing business with Iran will have to choose between the IRGC and having access to Western financial systems and assets:
No one has given the Islamic Republic of Iran a greater opportunity to make a Deal than me. TRAGICALLY, for them, they have failed to take it. Therefore, today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY! This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale. Their navy is gone, their air force is destroyed, their military factories are now rubble, their currency is worthless, and their country is hanging by a thread. Today, I am also announcing that ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences. Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies — It all needs to stop NOW. You know who you are. This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat. These maniacs are on the ropes, and these HISTORIC MEASURES will cripple them and their ability to project terror worldwide. IRAN WILL NEVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON. THANK YOU FOR YOUR ATTENTION TO THIS MATTER. President DONALD J. TRUMP
"You know who you are." Well, we all know who they are. They are China, Russia, Oman, Qatar, and most importantly for Iran, the UAE – whose emirates probably didn't need a threat from Trump to cut off the Iranians after the IRGC's attacks on their infrastructure. The UAE has long been the IRGC's financial proxy, helping it avoid sanctions largely driven by the US and adopted to some degree by the EU as well.
China has deep investments in the US market and will likely avoid a direct confrontation with Trump that could lead to a disruption of their business. Russia doesn't do much business with the West at this point, so Vladimir Putin will shrug at the threat. The real pressure point is Dubai, and the Wall Street Journal reports that it may take some arm-twisting despite the emirates' anger at the IRGC:
The United Arab Emirates said late Tuesday that it has suspended financial and economic transactions with Iran, potentially threatening Tehran’s access to a major source of imports and a financial back door to the world.
The move follows weeks of Trump administration cajoling of the U.A.E. to crack down on Iranian financial networks operating in the country, telling Emirati officials that targeting money flows linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps could have a greater impact on Tehran than the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, according to people familiar with the matter. ...
If implemented broadly, the U.A.E. step could significantly curb Tehran’s access to foreign currency and global trade networks as the Iranian economy buckles under soaring inflation, sanctions and wartime disruption. The Trump administration hopes that could increase pressure on Iran to strike a deal.
Are we still talking about a deal? Perhaps, but by this point, Trump has to recognize that the IRGC will never offer a deal in good faith. This is more about regime collapse at this point. The US can't force regime change from the air or sea, at least not directly, but a complete economic blockade may force a collapse and a popular revolt against the tyrannical and murderous regime.
That will require the UAE to join the US in this economic warfare fully. However, Dubai values its status as a financial Casablanca, and they may be more invested in playing both sides against the middle:
But severing those links will be difficult. Much of the activity is deliberately obscured. U.S. sanctions orders in recent years show that oil revenues, foreign-currency trades and payments for Iranian entities have long moved through shell companies and exchange houses in Dubai, often without an Iranian name appearing on the transaction.
Cutting off Iran would also require Emirati authorities to crack down much more aggressively on opaque financial and trading activity, which could hurt Dubai’s role as a freewheeling global hub for commerce, capital and re-exports.
Trump will have to convince the UAE that its long-term financial prospects also hinge on US protection for its shipping. Trump has one advantage in this situation that Bush lacked: a fully robust American oil production industry that exports enough to greatly influence global oil prices. The Iranian blockade and the arrest of Nicolas Maduro have cut deeply into black-market oil resources. That would normally benefit legit producers like the UAE, but it also makes their output less of a card to play against the West.
The UAE will have to play along, at least for now and at least to some nominal degree. If the emirates truly want to put an end to the risk factors that the IRGC has created for the last 47 years, they'll do so enthusiastically.

Trump Announces Increased Economic Pressure Against Iran. Oil Prices Jump.
Both Brent crude and West Texas Intermediate were climbing around 3%.
Oil prices are climbing on Thursday as prospects of an end to the war in Iran got dimmer following President Donald Trump's announcement that the U.S. will carry out an "economic D-Day" against Tehran.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, gained around 3% at 8:40 a.m. ET, clocking in at $94.33 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, gained 3.10% at the same time and stood at $87.01 at the same time.
In a social media post, Trump said that Washington will launch the "most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country."
"This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale," Trump said, also threatening large "economic consequences" for "ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran."
"This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat. These maniacs are on the ropes, and these HISTORIC MEASURES will cripple them and their ability to project terror worldwide," Trump added.
Iran dismissed the remarks, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling it a diversion from America's own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs."
"Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat—and enmity of Iranians. US economic terrorism threatens global economy and sovereignty worldwide," Araghchi added, citing an article noting that the U.S. national debt has crossed the $40 trillion mark.
In the meantime, a new report detailed that the U.S. military is carrying out missions to help vessels transit the Strait of Hormuz despite Iran's blockade.
Citing officials familiar with the matter, Axios detailed on Thursday that the strategy has managed to guarantee the shipping of about 10 millions of barrels a day.
Overall, between 15 and 20 tankers are entering and exiting the waterway at night through a channel along the coast of Oman.
U.S. forces are not only escorting the vessels, but also helping them pick up oil from countries in the region and then exit.
"We have been controlling the southern lane of the Strait of Hormuz for two months now. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps can be a nuisance, but they don't control the strait. We do," an official told the outlet.

sources.news_title: Iran dismisses Trump's 'Economic D-Day' threats
Iran’s Araghchi Calls Trump’s New Economic Pressure Campaign a Failed Policy
sources.text:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has described US President Donald Trump’s latest economic pressure campaign against Tehran as a failed policy, accusing Washington of using economic pressure to divert attention from its own financial problems.
Araghchi said in a post on X on Thursday that continued US pressure would only deepen hostility among Iranians and bring what he described as another defeat for Washington.
His remarks came after Trump announced what he called a major new economic campaign against Iran, warning countries and entities that continue doing business with Tehran that they could face severe economic consequences. Trump said the United States would pursue what he described as unprecedented economic pressure and isolation of Iran.
Araghchi accused Washington of “economic terrorism,” saying the US measures threatened the wider global economy. He argued that the campaign was intended to distract from mounting US debt and rising interest costs, echoing his earlier criticism of Washington’s economic policies.
The latest escalation comes as efforts to resolve the conflict between Washington and Tehran remain stalled. The war, which began in February, has disrupted energy markets and sharply reduced shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a major global oil transit route. Oil prices have risen in recent days amid renewed uncertainty over the conflict and the future of the waterway.
Trump’s announcement marks a shift toward intensified economic pressure as the United States seeks to force Tehran to make concessions. Washington has warned that countries helping Iran evade sanctions or maintain significant commercial ties with Tehran could also face penalties. Iran, however, has continued to reject what it describes as pressure and demands for surrender.
The latest exchange also underscores the widening gap between the two sides as diplomatic efforts remain uncertain. Iran has said it remains open to diplomacy but has rejected negotiations under what it considers unacceptable conditions, while Washington has continued to demand major changes in Tehran’s nuclear and regional policies.
With the conflict approaching its sixth month and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz still well below normal levels, further economic pressure on Iran could have broader consequences for regional trade, energy supplies and global markets.

sources.news_title: Trump announces 'most crushing' economic sanctions on Iran
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has announced that his administration was imposing the “most crushing economic operation” on Iran, a move analysts say shows the frustration of the American leader as his government makes no progress in the Iran war.
In a post on Truth Social early Thursday, Mr Trump said the sanctions will target “any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran.”
The US has imposed tough economic sanctions on Iran for over 40 years, and it remains to be seen how this new announcement will make any difference.
Mr Trump did not provide specifics on the nature of the expected US sanctions.
|  |  | 
|---|---|
However, Iran’s Foreign Minister, Abbas Araghchi, dismissed Mr Trump’s latest threats in a post on X, calling it a “diversion from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs.”
He stated that the “so-called ‘Economic D-Day’” would only bring further defeat to Washington.
“Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat—and enmity of Iranians. US economic terrorism threatens the global economy and sovereignty worldwide,” he wrote.
The Iranian Parliament Speaker, Mohammad Ghalibaf, also said the US was seeking an “honourable exit” from the Middle East while promoting a “new regional order”.
Mr Trump’s announcement also comes less than 24 hours after the UAE, a US ally, said it was ending all trade and economic cooperation with Iran.
It accused the country of launching ballistic missiles at the Gulf nation this week, an attack Iran denied, saying it could have been a false flag operation by the US or Israel.
According to analysts, the UAE’s embargo is likely to significantly affect Iran, which relies heavily on its neighbour for critical imports and access to financial markets.
ALSO READ: Trump admits to secret plane swap over Iranian threat
The US war with Iran has now lasted almost seven months.
On Monday, the Iran-US MoU, signed on 17 June, expired. It marked the end of a 60-day deadline during which both countries were supposed to end the war and reach an agreement on Iran’s nuclear programme.
PREMIUM TIMES previously reported that Mr Trump demanded that Tehran “put up the white flag of surrender.”
He also threatened to make the Strait of Hormuz US territory.
“After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States,” Mr Trump said.

sources.news_title: Iran-U.S. Economic Tensions: A Clash of Strategies
sources.text:
Iran-U.S. Economic Tensions: A Clash of Strategies
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi claims U.S. ‘Economic D-Day’ against Iran is a diversion from its own economic issues. Despite U.S. President Donald Trump's declaration of imposing the most severe economic measures against Iran, Araqchi insists further pressure will not succeed.
In a strong rebuttal to the United States' economic measures, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi labeled the so-called 'Economic D-Day' as a mere distraction from America's internal challenges.
U.S. President Donald Trump had earlier proclaimed the initiation of what he described as the 'most crushing economic operation' against a nation, specifically targeting Iran.
Araqchi expressed confidence that any additional pressure from the United States would be ineffective, maintaining Iran's stance amidst ongoing tensions.
(With inputs from agencies.)

sources.news_title: Trump has a new plan to crush Iran’s economy. But will he stay the course?
sources.text:
President Donald Trump is rolling out yet another Iran war strategy in familiar fashion: with an all-caps threat.
But the world will, as usual, have to wait to see whether he folds when the political costs pile up.
Trump on Wednesday promised “the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY” in a Truth Social post.
His new approach is something of a face-saver after he failed to bomb the Islamic Republic into surrender or to coax it to nuclear talks with sweeteners in a memorandum of understanding. It’s the latest dizzying twist in a conflict that has spawned more tactical shifts and course reversals than it’s possible to count.
The president has halted all conversations with Iran, and CNN reports his team has told political allies he’s settling into a war of economic attrition that he believes will demolish Iran’s economy and compel its capitulation.
“Right now, I think the situation is so good,” Trump said Wednesday of a war that he declared won after a few days but is now deep into its sixth month.
In a later social media post, he pledged to crack down on any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran. He wrote: “Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies — It all needs to stop NOW.”
“You know who you are,” the president added.
Many analysts are skeptical that the revolutionary regime in Tehran, known for inflicting intense repression and economic duress on civilians, will back down in its existential struggle with the US. After all, it’s endured decades of some of the world’s most punitive economic sanctions.
“Those who think that Iran will collapse under the pressure, I think they are mistaken, despite the economic situation,” said Daniel Citrinowicz, who served in Israel Defense Intelligence, including as head of the Iran branch in the Research and Analysis Division. Citrinowicz told CNN International on Tuesday there’s no sign Iran is easing its strategy of trying to pressure Trump through international markets. He added that while economic pressure could impose severe costs on Iran, “At the end of the day, I don’t see the Iranian calculus changing because of this pressure.”
What Trump must change
To make any progress, Trump will not simply have to change that calculus in Tehran. He must first change his own behavior.
Destroying Iran’s economy would take months or even years. It would call for the kind of strategic patience that Trump almost never shows. Iran will not be alone if it gambles that the president will tire of his new plan long before it shows results.
Trump’s new approach may also depend on a diplomatic shift.
The White House is putting huge faith in military power to enforce a blockade on Iran’s ships and ports — epitomized by his misleading social media post this week declaring the Strait of Hormuz a new US territory. But a truly effective attempt to isolate Iran implies a major effort, spanning the Gulf, Europe and Asia.
There are plausible ways that the administration could impose genuine pain on Iran’s regime.
Hudson Institute Senior Fellow Ludovic Hood advocates a regional and international squeeze on Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps revenues and a new move against its regional proxy network. In a recent Wall Street Journal op-ed, he called for strengthened US ties with governments in Baghdad and Beirut to challenge Tehran’s power across the Middle East and advised Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to turn up economic heat on China, a major purchaser of Iranian oil. Hood argued that sustained economic pressure would exacerbate inflation and capital flight, triggering a banking crisis that could loosen the regime’s grip.
A blockade would be even more effective if the US enlisted allies to shut down the web of clandestine economic arrangements and trade routes Tehran has built to evade sanctions. But such cooperation is hardly in the administration’s wheelhouse. Washington’s diplomacy on Iran, led by Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, has often been naive.
And the US president alienated allies by starting a war that threatened their national and economic security interests — then berated them for not joining in. This week, he threatened to bomb Oman over its stance in talks with Iran seeking to reopen the strait.
A total lockdown of Iran’s economy would not come without grave choices for Trump. For example, one impactful move would be to impose sanctions on Chinese banks involved in transactions over Iran’s illicit oil sales. But Trump will welcome China’s President Xi Jinping for a state visit in September — a highlight of his year. It would be a major surprise if he sours the atmosphere before then.
Will Trump stay the course or bluff and fold?
Even if Trump is willing to wait for his economic warfare to smother Iran, there’s another third variable: Tehran gets to respond.
It knows Trump is vulnerable just over two months from the midterms. And it seems bent on humiliating him just as completely as it humiliated President Jimmy Carter during the hostage crisis before the 1980 election.
Iran therefore has a powerful political rationale for denying Trump’s bid to quiet the war during the fall campaign. And it also has a geopolitical incentive to escalate in order to preserve its major war gain of being able to slow ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz. New drone or missile attacks on shipping would push up economic costs for American voters and remind them how much they hate the war. If the president were to respond, he’d worsen the crisis. If he held back, he’d look weak.
A hot war or an economic one will leave openings for Democrats. “I’m not interested in a war of economic attrition with Iran, where the American people are the ones paying the price on our side of the equation, at the gas pump and at the grocery store,” Democratic Rep. James Walkinshaw told CNN News Central on Tuesday.
Despite Trump’s latest social media outburst, there’s still no endgame within sight.
And the president is still wrestling with the question that entraps him: Will Americans’ tolerance for the fallout from the war run out before the regime’s does?

sources.news_title: Could Trump’s Iran Economic Threat Deepen the Global Economic Crisis?
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump has warned that countries providing any form of economic support to Iran could face severe consequences, escalating Washington’s pressure campaign as the nearly six month old Iran war continues to disrupt regional trade and global energy markets.
Trump threatened what he described as economic warfare and unprecedented isolation against countries whose financial institutions, businesses, airports or governments provide Iran with what he called a “lifeline.”
The warning comes as Washington seeks to pressure Tehran toward a broader agreement on its nuclear programme while maintaining economic and military pressure on Iran.
Why Is Trump Threatening Countries Supporting Iran?
Trump’s warning represents an attempt to further isolate Iran economically by making third countries think twice before maintaining commercial, financial or logistical links with Tehran.
Stay ahead of the geopolitical week.

Iran has already endured decades of U.S. sanctions, dating back to the 1979 Islamic Revolution. Additional restrictions could therefore target the remaining channels through which Tehran conducts international trade and receives financial support.
However, Trump did not specify what measures would be imposed or which countries could be targeted.
That uncertainty is significant because several countries involved in economic relations with Iran are also important U.S. partners.
Could U.S. Pressure Affect American Allies?
The threat could create a difficult diplomatic problem for Washington.
The United Arab Emirates, which hosts a major U.S. military base, announced on Tuesday that it was suspending trade activities, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran until further notice.
The UAE has also played a role in regional diplomacy.
Trump’s warning therefore risks putting pressure not only on Iran but also on countries that have maintained economic or diplomatic channels with Tehran.
If Washington begins imposing penalties on allies for continuing limited economic relations with Iran, tensions within the U.S.-led regional coalition could increase.
Why Is China Central to the Iran Sanctions Debate?
China represents the biggest challenge to any attempt to completely isolate Iran.
According to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler, China buys more than 80% of Iran’s shipped oil.
That makes Beijing crucial to Tehran’s ability to continue generating energy revenues despite U.S. sanctions.
At the same time, China is an important economic rival of the United States and a major supplier of critical materials, including rare earth minerals.
Washington therefore faces a difficult calculation.
Aggressively targeting Chinese purchases of Iranian oil could further damage U.S. economic relations with Beijing and potentially provoke retaliation.
How Has the UAE Responded?
The UAE’s decision to suspend economic activity with Iran illustrates how the conflict is already affecting regional commerce.
The move followed the UAE defence ministry’s statement that it had detected two missiles launched from Iran that fell into the sea.
Iran rejected the report as baseless.
The episode highlights the broader security dilemma facing Gulf states. Many host U.S. military forces while maintaining economic relationships with Iran, leaving them vulnerable to pressure from both Washington and Tehran.
Is Diplomacy Between Washington and Tehran Still Alive?
The diplomatic picture remains unclear.
The United States and Iran have announced ceasefire agreements twice, in April and June, but both quickly collapsed.
Trump said on Tuesday that no talks were taking place with Iran.
A day earlier, however, his son-in-law and special envoy Jared Kushner said discussions were continuing and were potentially more substantial than before.
Iran has also indicated that it remains open to dialogue.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, said Iran does not confuse negotiations with surrender and argued that military pressure and sanctions would not force Tehran to abandon its position.
What Does Trump Want From Iran?
Trump is seeking a new and more restrictive agreement covering Iran’s nuclear programme.
Washington wants to secure Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile and impose tighter restrictions on its nuclear energy and research activities.
Trump previously withdrew the United States from the 2015 nuclear agreement in 2018 and restored sanctions against Tehran.
Iran, meanwhile, maintains that its nuclear programme is peaceful and has long denied seeking nuclear weapons.
Could More Sanctions Hurt the Global Economy?
The consequences could extend beyond Iran.
Iran remains an important energy producer, while the Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most strategically important energy routes.
Before the conflict, roughly one fifth of globally traded oil passed through the waterway.
The war has already disrupted shipping and contributed to volatility in global energy markets.
If additional sanctions restrict Iran’s oil exports or provoke further retaliation, energy prices could face renewed upward pressure.
That could feed into transportation, manufacturing and consumer prices globally.
Analysis: Economic Warfare Could Become a Broader Geopolitical Battle
Trump’s latest warning demonstrates that the Iran conflict is increasingly being fought through economic pressure as much as military power.
Washington’s objective is clear: make the economic cost of supporting Tehran sufficiently high that governments and companies distance themselves from Iran.
But the strategy carries significant risks.
The United States cannot easily isolate Iran without confronting the countries that remain commercially connected to it. China is the most obvious example, given its dominant role in purchasing Iranian oil.
This creates a dilemma for Washington. Targeting Beijing could strengthen pressure on Tehran, but it could simultaneously intensify an already difficult U.S.-China economic confrontation.
The same problem exists with U.S. allies in the Gulf. Countries such as the UAE must balance their security partnerships with Washington against their geographic proximity and economic relationships with Iran.
The biggest risk is therefore that economic warfare begins producing consequences beyond its intended target.
Trump may be seeking to isolate Iran, but an aggressive sanctions campaign could instead widen the economic front of the war, strain U.S. alliances and intensify pressure on already fragile global energy markets.
With information from Reuters.

sources.news_title: President Trump Declares ‘Economic D-Day’ Against Iran, Threatens Countries Providing Tehran a Lifeline
sources.text:
President Trump Declares ‘Economic D-Day’ Against Iran, Threatens Countries Providing Tehran a Lifeline
President Donald Trump declared an “Economic D-Day” against Iran, announcing what he described as an unprecedented campaign of economic warfare and threatening severe consequences for countries that continue providing Tehran with financial or commercial lifelines.
He argued that Iran had failed to take advantage of opportunities to reach an agreement with the United States and would now face sweeping efforts to further isolate its economy.
“No one has given the Islamic Republic of Iran a greater opportunity to make a Deal than me. TRAGICALLY, for them, they have failed to take it,” President Trump wrote in a social media post.
“Therefore, today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY!” he added. “This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.”

The president also put other countries on notice that maintaining economic links with Tehran could bring consequences of their own.
“ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” Trump said.
He specifically demanded an end to oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, and front companies.
President Trump called on US allies to join Washington in isolating Tehran, declaring, “This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat.”
“IRAN WILL NEVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON,” he added.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi dismissed Trump’s announcement as “a distraction from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt and rising prices.”
“Doubling down on a failed policy will only lead to another defeat,” Araqchi said. “US economic terrorism threatens the global economy and sovereignty around the world.”

sources.news_title: US ‘economic D-Day’ diversion from its own crisis: Araghchi
sources.text:
In a post on his X account on Thursday, Iran's top diplomat warned that continuing failed US policies would deepen Washington’s economic difficulties and fuel further hostility toward Iran.
“The so-called ‘Economic D-Day’ is a diversion from America's own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs,” he wrote.
“Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat—and enmity of Iranians. US economic terrorism threatens global economy and sovereignty worldwide,” Araghchi added.
He also attached photos of reports highlighting the unprecedented growth of US national debt, including headlines noting that the debt had reached $40 trillion after decades of borrowing.
The reports described the $40 trillion milestone as a serious fiscal concern and cited data showing total US government debt at $40.05 trillion, up $2.90 trillion, or 7.8%, from the same period a year earlier. One of the graphics also tracked the US national debt by month since 1993.
Iran's top diplomat dismissed the US administration’s so-called “Economic D-Day” as an attempt to divert attention from Washington’s mounting debt and economic problems.

sources.news_title: Trump: U.S. launching 'economic warfare' against Iran
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. will begin what President Donald Trump said would be an unprecedented economic warfare operation against Iran, after faulting the country for failing to take its chance to make a deal with him.
“Therefore, today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY! This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale,” Trump said in a social media post Wednesday.
Trump’s post didn’t specify the measures the U.S. would take. Iran is already subject to widespread U.S. sanctions, and the American military has sought to enforce a maritime blockade on the country.
The Trump administration has in recent weeks shifted from military options to economic pressure on Iran was the war drags on with negotiations deadlocked. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had openly warned the U.S. was preparing to unleash unprecedented measures to squeeze the Islamic Republic’s economy.
Trump said Wednesday the pressure campaign would extend to Iran’s trading partners, warning that “ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences.”
He listed examples of aid to Iran that its economic partners should cease, including exchange houses, cash transfers and swap lines, ship registries, front companies and oil smuggling.
That firm red line could invite tough decisions for the Trump administration given Iran’s ties to China and test its appetite for going after entities tied to Beijing.
Oil held four days of gains, with West Texas Intermediate for October trading above $84 a barrel, while Brent closed near $92.
Trump’s announcement comes a day after the United Arab Emirates severed economic ties with Iran, citing “escalations that undermine regional and international peace and security.”
While U.S. allies have been reluctant to join the military campaign Trump and Israel began in late February, the president called on them to help choke off Iran economically.
“This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat,” he said.
With assistance from Jennifer A. Dlouhy and Magdalena Del Valle.

Trump's Iran squeeze hinges on UAE crackdown on Dubai financial networks - report
The Trump administration has told Emirati officials that targeting money flows linked to the IRGC could hit Tehran harder than the US naval blockade
President Donald Trump's effort to squeeze Iran economically depends heavily on curbing one of the country's largest financial lifelines, Dubai, the Wall Street Journal reported. The United Arab Emirates said late Tuesday it had suspended financial and economic transactions with Iran, a move that could threaten Tehran's access to a major source of imports and a financial back door to the world.
The move follows weeks of Trump administration pressure on the UAE to crack down on Iranian financial networks operating in the country, people familiar with the matter told the Journal. US officials told Emirati counterparts that targeting money flows tied to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps could have a greater impact on Iran than the US naval blockade of its ports. Washington has also urged the UAE to take tougher action against sanctioned Iranian entities and covert networks operating in the Emirates during the war.
"Today, I am also announcing that ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences," Trump wrote on social media. "Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies. It all needs to stop NOW. You know who you are."
Emirati officials view the latest measures as a gradual escalation rather than a full break with Tehran, according to people familiar with the matter. The UAE is expected to proceed step by step, starting with new cargo restrictions and potentially expanding to a broader crackdown on Iranian-linked entities if the Revolutionary Guard continues its strikes.
UAE policymakers are concerned that Washington's push for deeper economic pain on Iran could hurt the segment of Gulf economies reliant on tourism and trade rather than oil, and could provoke further Iranian military retaliation, the people said. Emirati officials also want to preserve some channels to Tehran to retain a diplomatic option if the US pressure campaign fails.
Suggested articles
The UAE action follows weeks of escalating tensions, including what Emirati officials say were Iranian attacks on seven of its ships this month. On Tuesday, Iran fired two ballistic missiles toward the UAE, triggering the country's air defenses; the UAE Defense Ministry said the missiles targeted maritime traffic and fell into the sea.
Before the war, the UAE was Iran's largest source of imports, supplying more than 30 percent of the country's total, about $21 billion, in 2024, according to the World Trade Organization. In 2024, $9 billion passing through US bank correspondent accounts appeared tied to clandestine Iranian financial activity, with UAE-based firms, mostly in Dubai, receiving 62 percent of those funds, according to the Treasury Department.

sources.news_title: Trump declares economic warfare, threatens ‘any country’ helping Iran
sources.text:
Trump declares economic warfare, threatens ‘any country’ helping Iran
WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday he was launching a major new campaign to target Iran’s economy and threatened “tremendous” punishment on any country that helps or does business with the Islamic republic.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump announced what he called the “most crushing economic operation” against Iran, ramping up pressure on Tehran amid a deadlock in negotiations to end the military conflict between the two countries.
Trump’s announcement came hours after the United Arab Emirates, a critical trade partner for Iran, suspended all financial ties with the country, accusing it of launching two ballistic missiles towards its waters.
Tehran denied the claim, calling it a “false-flag operation”.
Trump said Iran has “failed to take” the opportunity to make a deal, and would face “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale”.
“Today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY! This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
“I am also announcing that ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” he said. “Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies — it all needs to stop NOW. You know who you are. This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat.”
He did not specify what punishment countries helping Iran would face, and no country other than Iran was mentioned by name.
The president’s comments come nearly a week after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US would impose economic isolation on the country “like the world has never seen before.”
The intensified economic pressure campaign comes as the war that the US and Israel started in February nears its sixth month with no immediate diplomatic or military off-ramp in sight.
Trump is also facing renewed domestic political scrutiny over the war with November mid-term elections quickly approaching.
This is not the first time that Trump has threatened Iran with economic sanctions.
His administration has waged an economic pressure campaign against Iran, under the banner of Operation Economic Fury, following the launch of the US-Israel war on the country in February.
The US has already imposed sweeping sanctions on Iran’s oil, shipping and financial sectors, seeking to cut off the revenue Tehran earns from energy exports. It has also imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and targeted companies, brokers and tankers accused of helping Iran sell its oil abroad.
There was no immediate response from Iranian officials, but state media dismissed Trump’s announcement as nothing new.
The IRIB state broadcaster said it followed “the failure of military aggression” while the semi-official Tasnim news agency said the announcement was “not a new development”. It said the US “has been trying for years to block any financial and economic ties with Iran” but that Tehran has “learned how to circumvent these restrictions and has become very skilled at doing so”.
The semi-official Fars news agency also dismissed Trump’s claims as “delusional”, saying that the US had repeatedly voiced assertions of Iran’s “imminent collapse” and military destruction without delivering concrete results.
Despite a recent lull in missile strikes, Iran has continued to impose an effective blockade on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, after a frame US-Iran deal to reopen the vital corridor collapsed.
In recent days, both sides have said messages were being exchanged, but Trump on Tuesday insisted talks were off and posted a message on social media suggesting the strait could be a “NEW US Territory.”

“Tragically, for them, they have failed to take it. Therefore, today, I am announcing the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country,” he continued.

“Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies—it all needs to stop now,” he stated. “You know who you are. This will be an economic D-Day.”
He called on all U.S. allies to “isolate and defeat the Iran threat.”
“These maniacs are on the ropes,” he said. “These historic measures will cripple them and their ability to project terror worldwide. Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) August 19, 2026
On Tuesday, Trump said Washington was not currently negotiating with Tehran and that no talks are scheduled.
“There are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled, with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that “the naval blockade remains in full force and effect. The Hormuz Strait is open and operating. All water mines have been removed or detonated.”
Tehran rejected those assertions, maintaining that the waterway remains under Iranian authority and will stay shut until Washington yields to its terms.
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s top negotiator, said in Tehran on Tuesday that the strategic maritime passage would not reopen until the United States satisfies the Islamic Republic’s demands, including the removal of the naval blockade on its southern ports.
On Monday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters that the 60-day negotiating period with the U.S. had “completely lost its relevance,” according to a translation by the semi-official ISNA news agency.
Baghaei said the June 17 memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran provided “merely a 60-day window for talks on two axes, sanctions relief and the nuclear issue, which could be extended if no result was reached.” He claimed the substantive negotiations envisioned under the agreement never began.
According to a Wall Street Journal report on Sunday, Iran spent the two months since signing the memorandum preparing for a wider conflict. Tehran strengthened the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ control over the country’s conventional armed forces, increased missile and drone production and coordinated plans for expanded attacks by Iranian-backed terrorist groups across the region, according to the report.

sources.news_title: Trump warns of consequences for any country that supports Iran
sources.text:
Trump warns of economic consequences for any country that supports Iran
- By Reuters -
- Aug 20, 2026
U.S. President Donald Trump warned of economic consequences against any country that provided “any type of lifeline to Iran” as the U.S. looks to resolve a war it began alongside Israel nearly six months ago.
Thousands of people have been killed in the war, which quickly drew in countries across the Gulf, and global markets have been shocked as Iran flexed its ability to control shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world’s traded oil passed before February.
The U.S. and Iran have twice announced ceasefire agreements, in April and June, designed to restore the free flow of shipping through Hormuz to pre-war levels on the way towards ending the conflict, but both quickly crumbled even as Israel has largely withdrawn from the fighting.
In a message posted on social media on Wednesday evening, Trump promised “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale,” although details were scant. Iran has weathered continuous punishing economic sanctions for nearly 50 years, since the Islamic Revolution of 1979.
“ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” Trump wrote.
Trump’s social media threats and announcements do not always get fleshed out or successfully acted upon as written, and he did not specify what specific steps the U.S. would take against such a country, which would appear to include U.S. allies that have helped mediate peace talks, and he did not list any country by name.
On Tuesday, the United Arab Emirates, which hosts a major U.S. military base, announced it was suspending all trade activities, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran until further notice. The announcement came after the UAE defense ministry said it had detected two missiles launched from Iran that fell into the sea, a report Iran dismissed as baseless.
China buys more than 80% of Iran’s shipped oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler, but for the U.S. to engage in further economic warfare with China, a major exporter to the U.S. including of vital rare-earth minerals, risks retaliation.
Iran remains open to dialogue with the U.S. but does not confuse negotiations with surrender, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, said on Tuesday, according to the semi-official Fars news agency. Mokhber said military pressure and sanctions would not break Iran’s resolve.
On Tuesday, Trump said no talks, opens new tab were taking place with Iran. A day earlier, Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and special envoy, struck an upbeat tone, saying talks with Iran were still underway and were “probably more robust” than ever.
Trump wants to seize Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium and is seeking a new, more restrictive agreement curbing Iran’s nuclear energy and research programs, to replace the one he unilaterally withdrew the U.S. from in 2018. Iran, a non-proliferation treaty signatory, has for decades said its nuclear programs are peaceful.

sources.news_title: Trump warns 'economic consequences' for nations helping Iran
sources.text:
Trump warns 'economic consequences' for nations helping Iran
Published August 20, 2026last updated August 20, 2026
What you need to know
This blog is now closed. Here are the latest developments from the Iran war and the Middle East on Thursday, August 20:
- US President Donald Trump has announced the "most crushing economic operation" ever against Iran
- Trump hs said any country providing “any type of lifeline to Iran” will face "tremendous" economic repercussions
- Iran's media has dismissed Trump's threat
- US sanctions on Iran are "economic terrorism," Tehran has said
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
US Treasury sanctions 10 individuals for alleged cash smuggling for Hezbollah
The United States Treasury on Thursday put sanctions on 10 individuals it accuses of involvement in smuggling networks for Lebanon's Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group.
"[Hezbollah] and its allies exploit financing schemes including oil smuggling, illicit shipping, commodities sales, and bulk cash smuggling to generate and move funds across the region," the Treasury said in its statement.
Among those targeted is a Turkish businessman the Treasury accuses of using Turkey-base exchange houses to move cash between other countries in the region and Hezbollah's base in Lebanon.
Washington also redesignated Hezbollah as a terrorist organization, citing "service to the Iranian regime under the command of Iran's [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) - Quds Force]"
The Quds Force is an elite unit of the IRGC in charge of its overseas operations. Earlier this year, the EU designated Iran's Revolutionary Guard a terror group.
US: Economic isolation will 'collapse' regime in Iran
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Thursday that Washington believed economic pressure would successfully bring about regime change in Iran.
"It is going to work in Iran and we are going to collapse this regime," Bessent told US broadcaster CNBC.
He said that the US would work to isolate Iran economically.
"This is going to be the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world. And we are going to them and saying you are either with us or against us," he said.
He said that the strong economic pressure would make "large-scale" military operations unnecessary.
"If we are doing the maximum economic pressure, then that means that likely there will not be a large-scale kinetic restart, but I will emphasize that is for no," he said.
Asked whether the United States would also pressure China to join in the drive to isolate Iran, he said "many conversations are best to have in private."
Iran's Foreign Ministry condemns new US sanctions as 'economic terrorism'
Iran's Foreign Ministry strongly condemned new US economic and trade sanctions on Thursday.
The ministry said that the measures amount to "economic terrorism" and crimes against humanity, adding that the sanctions will hurt ordinary Iranians.
"Sanctions and economic pressure are the other side of the coin of war and military aggression," the ministry said in its statement.
It comes after US President Donald Trump threatened "tremendous economc consequences" for "any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran."
Iran executes Afghan national over January protests
Iran on Thursday executed an Afghan citizen convicted over the killing of police officers during anti-government protests in January.
The Mizan Online portal, which is tied to the Iranian judiciary, reported that Ghaem Hosseini was a foreign national without providing further details.
It said he was convicted of "of drawing a weapon and causing fear and terror, creating widespread insecurity, acting against people's physical integrity and national security in a manner that seriously disrupted public order."
The Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHR) group said that the 21-year-old was from neighboring Afghanistan and was hanged at Isfahan central prison.
IHR said that Hosseini was accused of kicking a policeman. It added that Iranian authorities had not presented evidence that Hosseini had carried out any acts that led to the death of police officers.
He is the fifth person to be hanged over the case involving the death of four police officers in Isfahan in central Iran in January.
He is the second Afghan national to be executed over the protests.
Iran is home to the largest Afghan diaspora population in the world, numbering over 4 million.
Dozens executed over protests
IHR says at least 28 people involved in the protest wave of December 2025 - January 2026 have been executed since March 19.
It said that hundreds of others have been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty.
The mass protests in Iran began on 28 December 2025, with millions taking to the streets as demonstrations peaked in January.
The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) said at least 7,000 people were killed in the ensuing crackdown, some 6,500 of them protesters and 214 being security personnel.
Turkey, Egypt, Qatar call for compliance with Gaza ceasefire, condemn Israeli strikes
Turkey, Egypt and Qatar on Thursday condemned recent Israeli strikes on Gaza in a joint statement.
They called on the international community and the US-led Board of Peace to take necessary steps to ensure compliance with the ceasefire in the Palestinian enclave.
"The mediating countries underline that the intensification of Israeli attacks undermines regional and international efforts at a critical juncture," the statement read.
"The mediating countries stress the imperative for Israel to fully comply with all its obligations under the ceasefire agreement and to refrain from actions that could further undermine the ceasefire and escalate tensions," the three countries stressed.
"The mediating countries reiterate their call on the international community and the Board of Peace ... to take the necessary steps to ensure compliance with th ceasefire and to exert effective pressure to prevent further escalation."
What is the Board of Peace's plan for Gaza?
Last month, the Board of Peace said it had reached a deal for the complete disarmament of Hamas, classified by multiple countries as a terrorist organization, and other armed groups in Gaza.
The 15-point road map aimed at ending the war calls for Israeli troops to withdraw as Hamas gives up its weapons.
Weeks later, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Israel rejected the deal, calling instead for the "genuine" disarmament of Hamas before any Israeli withdrawal.
Qatar, Turkey and Egypt are all founding members of the 27-country Board of Peace, which was established by US President Donald Trump in January.
Vatican expresses 'serious concerns' about implementation of Israel-Lebanon deal
The Vatican expressed its concern on Thursday around the implementation of a US-brokered deal between Israel and Lebanon.
"The Holy See, whilst welcoming the signing of the document, has expressed serious concerns about the difficulties being encountered in implementing it, and has pledged its support for efforts to that end," the Vatican said.
The statement comes after Pope Leo XIV met with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the Vatican.
Aoun called on the Catholic Church to "support Lebanon's efforts to achieve a full Israeli withdrawal from the occupied Lebanese territories, paving the way for the reconstruction of what Israel has destroyed."
He also urged the Vatican to "continue their diplomatic efforts" to ensure Israel implements the terms of the US-brokered deal.
Lebanon's population is religiously diverse and has the largest concentration of Catholics in the Middle East, with members of the Maronite church particularly present in Beirut and parts of the country's northwest.
By convention, the post of Lebanon's president is filled by a Maronite Catholic.
What are the terms of the agreement between Lebanon and Israel?
The US-brokered framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon calls for the disarmament of the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group and the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces, alongside the deployment of the Lebanese army.
As part of its military operations, Israel treats an area 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) into Lebanese territory as a "security zone." Under the terms of the agreement, Israel is to gradually hand back "pilot zones" in the area to Lebanon.
Hezbollah has denounced the agreement, calling it a threat to Lebanon's sovereignty.
Israel has continued to strike Lebanon and engage in demolition operations in its southern regions since the agreement was reached.
Israel warns Turkey against 'dangerous adventures in Syria'
Turkey says it will continue supporting Syria's sovereignty after Israel bombed a Syrian air base and accused Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of dragging his country into "dangerous adventures" there.
Click here to read more about the tensions between Israel and Turkey over Syria.
Armed gunmen seize tanker in Gulf of Aden off Yemen
Armed gunmen seized a tanker in the Gulf of Aden off Yemen, maritime security agencies said Thursday.
"The tanker has reportedly been boarded by six armed persons, who are now in control of the vessel and redirecting it towards Somalia," the European Union's Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean (MSCIO) said.
United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) also reported the incident, saying that the tanker issued a distress call as it was approached 136 nautical miles east of Al Mukalla in Yemen.
UKMTO did not provide further details and did not say whether the tanker or it screw were safe.
Israelis begin moving into settlement evacuated in 2005
Israelis began moving into the settlement of Kadim in the occupied West Bank on Thursday, the Samaria Regional Council said.
The council is the administrative body that administers Israeli settlements in parts of the north of the occupied Palestinian territory. The area is home to some 50,000 Israeli settlers.
The council said that 30 families had moved into the reestablished settlement, hailing the move as a "historic milestone." They were accompanied by far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and regional council head Yossi Dagan.
"Twenty-one years after the crime of the expulsion from northern Samaria, today we have completed the rectification," Smotrich said, referring to the 2005 dismantlement of the settlement by Israeli authorities.
"These communities constitute a real security buffer for the entire state of Israel," he said.
He also vowed to establish another 19 settlements in the northern West Bank.
Smotrich himself lives in the settlement of Kedumim in the West Bank.
He also heads the Administration for Settlement Affairs, an agency that oversees settlement expansion and is part of the Defense Ministry.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.
Why did Israel evacuate West Bank settlements in 2005?
Kadim is one of four Israeli settlements — alongside Ganim, Sa-Nur and Homesh — in the northern West Bank that were evacuated by Israeli authorities under a 2005 unilateral disengagement plan.
The evacuation was largely carried out due to their isolation from major settlement blocs and proximity to densely populated Palestinian areas, including the major towns of Jenin and Nablus.
Kadim itself is located on a hilltop just 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) from Jenin.
The 2005 disengagement also included the evacuation of all 21 Israeli settlements in the Gaza Strip.
All four evacuated West Bank settlements have been reestablished by Israeli authorities over the course of 2025 and 2026.
Iran calls Trump's 'economic warfare' announcement 'diversion' from US domestic issues
Iran has slammed US President Donald Trump's "Economic D-Day" punishment plan against Tehran as a diversion from his country’s economic problems.
"The so-called ‘Economic D-Day’ is a diversion from America's own crisis: unprecedented debt and surging interest costs," Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X as he shared snippets of US media outlets reporting on the US gross national debt reaching $40 trillion.
He said Trump's latest announcement was a continuation of "failed policies".
"Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat — and enmity of Iranians," Araghchi said.
The Iranian foreign minister added that "global economy and sovereignty worldwide" was threatened by what he called "US economic terrorism."
Britain denounces tender launch for Israeli E1 settlement in West Bank
The United Kingdom has summoned Israel's charge d'affaires in London as it condemned Israel’s move to launch a tender for a controversial West Bank settlement project.
The plan would build 3,500 new apartments in an area known as E1, which lies between East Jerusalem and the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim. The new development would effectively split the West Bank into two parts.
Late on Tuesday, Israel's Land Authority published a tender for the building of the first 1,234 housing units in the project.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband on Wednesday called the move "an unacceptable and destructive act," saying that it would "endanger the viability of a two-state solution".
"I made clear to the Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar that the Israeli government must halt E1 plans immediately, retract the tender and stop all settlement expansion," Miliband said.
The UK, Germany, France and Italy had earlier cautioned companies against taking part in tenders for construction projects in the E1 and thereby engaging in "serious violations of international law."
Australia 'outraged' over Israel declining to open criminal probe in World Central Kitchen deaths
Australia on Thursday summoned Israel's ambassador to protest a decision by its military to not launch criminal investigations into the death of an Australian aid worker during a 2024 Israeli air strike on Gaza.
Australian national Lalzawmi "Zomi" Frankcom was among a group of seven World Central Kitchen employees killed on April 1, 2024 when their aid convoy was hit in an Israeli strike.
The attack had drawn widespread international condemnation.
On Wednesday, the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) said it had found no basis to probe the deaths of the charity's staff after a fact-finding and assessment procedure.
The IDF said in its report that it had mistakenly identified several individuals in the vehicles as Hamas militants and that the convoy deviated from its planned route. It concluded that "the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct."
Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who summoned Israeli ambassador Hillel Newman, said relations with Israel were "difficult" after the decision.
"This decision falls far short of the accountability we expect," Wong said, adding that Canberra was outraged.
Wong deemed Israel's move to not launch criminal proceedings into Frankcom and her colleagues' death as "especially insulting and hurtful" as it was announced on World Humanitarian Day.
"We do not have confidence" in Israel's investigation into the killings, she said. "The Australian government will continue to keep pressing Israel for justice."
Meanwhile, Newman after meeting Wong expressed "deep sorrow and grief" to Frankcom's family as he spoke to the media.
"Israel had no intention to attack or injure in any way the aid workers that were on the convoy," he stressed.
He said that Israel's decision was that there was no "criminal liability" and went on to say: "We must respect that conclusion."
Trump threatens Iran partners with economic punishment
US President Donald Trump has warned any country that supports Iran of economic consequences as war soon approaches its sixth month with no resolution in sight.
Trump said on his Truth Social platform on Wednesday that "ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS economic consequences."
The US leader described his move as "economic warfare" and "isolation" on an unprecedented scale as he stepped up an economic pressure campaign on Iran.
"Today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY!" he said, referring to the Islamic Republic in the superlatives-embellished post.
Trump said that nobody other than him had given Tehran what he called "a greater opportunity to make a deal".
"TRAGICALLY, for them, they have failed to take it," he said.
Trump said that Washington needed the support of all its allies to isolate Iran and counter the threat posed by the country.
He compared his plan to an "ECONOMIC D-DAY".
There were no details of what Trump’s economic steps against nations supporting Iran would look like, Trump also did not mention any country by name, other than Iran.
Iran media reacts to Trump’s "economic warfare" warning
Iran’s Fars news agency on Thursday called Trump’s latest economic threat the usual "psychological warfare and propaganda campaign,"
The country’s Tasnim news agency said the US presidents' announcement was "not a new development, as the United States has been trying for years to block any financial and economic ties with Iran."
Tehran has "learned how to circumvent these restrictions and has become very skilled at doing so," Tasnim said on Telegram.
Welcome to our coverage
Thank you for joining us as we bring you the latest edition of our rolling updates on the war in Iran and the wider Middle Eastern crisis.
But first here is a wrap up of the developments that took place in the region this week:
- US President Donald Trump emphasized that no talks or conversations between Washington and Tehran were being held
- The United Arab Emirates suspended trade ties with Iran after accusing the country of firing two ballistic missiles
- Human Rights Watch urged the United Nations to keep its international peacekeeping force in Lebanon, saying that a decision to end UNIFIL's mandate came before this year's war and the subsequent Israeli invasion of southern Lebanon
- The Israeli military announced criminal probes into two high-profile attacks during the Gaza war — the killings of 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in 2024 and 15 Palestinian paramedics in 2025
Follow along for more.

sources.news_title: Trump announces most crushing economic operation ever against Iran, issues warning to allies
sources.text:
World News
Trump announces most crushing economic operation ever against Iran, issues warning to allies
United States President Donald Trump has declared the commencement of the “most severe economic operation” against Iran.
This is as negotiations aimed at resolving the prolonged conflict between the two nations remain stalled.
In a message posted on Truth Social on Wednesday, Trump stated that Iran had “failed to seize” the opportunity to negotiate a deal and would face “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale.”
He further warned of sanctions against any nation that engages in business with Iran.
He said, “Any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences. Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies — it all needs to stop now.”
“You know who you are. This will be an Economic D-DAY, and we require all of our Allies to unite with the United States of America to isolate and overcome the Iran threat,” he wrote.
This is not the first instance in which Trump has issued threats of economic sanctions against Iran.
His administration has conducted a pressure campaign against Iran since April under the initiative known as Operation Economic Fury, aimed at isolating Tehran and obstructing its revenue sources.
The US has already imposed extensive sanctions on Iran’s oil, shipping and financial sectors, with the goal of severing the revenue Tehran generates from energy exports.
Additionally, it has established a naval blockade on Iranian ports and targeted companies, brokers and tankers accused of facilitating Iran’s oil sales abroad.

sources.news_title: Trump vows ‘tremendous’ economic costs for countries doing business with Iran
sources.text:
Trump has threatened countries doing business with Iran with “tremendous” economic consequences as the war continues.
Image: Xinhua
US President Donald Trump said Wednesday he was launching a major new campaign to target Iran's economy, threatening "tremendous" punishment on any country that helps or does business with the Islamic republic.
The intensified economic pressure campaign comes as the war nears its sixth month with no immediate diplomatic or military off-ramp in sight and the vital Strait of Hormuz still significantly choked-off.
With November elections quickly approaching, Trump is also facing renewed domestic scrutiny over the war's costs on US consumers and toll on the military.
"Today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY! This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
"ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences," he said.
He did not specify what punishment countries would face, and none other than Iran were mentioned by name.
He listed several activities that he said need to stop immediately: "oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies."
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had similarly said last week that the US would soon be ramping up efforts at economically isolating Iran, as part of a two-pronged approach with a US naval blockade.
"It will be a combination of economic isolation, like the world has never seen before," Bessent told conservative television network Newsmax.
The US Treasury has for months been carrying out an effort, dubbed Operation Economic Fury, aiming to cut off Iran's funding with targeted sanctions.
Iranian defiance
Iran has struck a defiant tone, having survived months of US military operations that failed to bring a decisive end to the war and has - according to US media reports - severely drawn down US munition stockpiles. The Pentagon has denied these reports.
The conflict broke out on February 28 with US-Israeli attacks on the Islamic republic, which retaliated with missile and drone strikes across the region.
Tehran's missile and drone threat has severely curtailed shipping traffic through the Strait, as a framework US-Iran deal to reopen it collapsed.
However, Trump earlier on Wednesday touted US military efforts to aid ships out of the strait, saying "right now, a lot of boats are coming through."
Digital media outlet Axios reported that US forces were facilitating the transit of 15 to 20 ships in and out of the Hormuz each night in recent weeks - carrying "roughly half the pre-war volume" of daily oil shipments.
In recent days, both sides have said messages were being exchanged, however Trump on Tuesday insisted talks were off and posted a message on social media suggesting the strait could be a "NEW U.S. Territory."
On Tuesday, the UAE announced that it was suspending all economic dealings with Iran after saying it had been targeted by two ballistic missiles.
The neighbours across the Gulf share deep cultural and historical ties, and the UAE - home to a sizable Iranian community - had been a major trading partner for US-sanctioned Iran, at least before the war.
"We need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat," Trump said Wednesday on Truth Social.
AFP

sources.news_title: Trump's Economic D-Day Threat Over Iran Branded A 'Complete S**t Show'
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s lengthy social media rant threatening an “ECONOMIC D-DAY” over Iran on Wednesday was ripped apart by critics who seemed to see right through his rhetoric.
Mere hours after bragging that the situation was “so good” with Iran, Trump promised the country would experience “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.” He also noted that any country that “allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences.”
“You know who you are,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat.”
Critics were quick to point out that the countries aiding Iran during the conflict were the same ones Trump often praises, including Russia. This would make it improbable that Trump would follow through with his ultimatum, thus continuing his pattern of walking back economic and military threats against Iran.
According to CNN’s Fareed Zakaria, Iran has been under international economic sanctions for decades, and there were few measures the U.S. could take outside of sanctioning or cutting off relations with Tehran’s largest trading partners.
“Iran’s largest trading partner is China; its second largest trading partner, I believe, is Russia. It also trades with North Korea, a little bit with India. These are not countries that the Trump administration has that much influence over,” Zakaria said on Wednesday’s edition of “Anderson Cooper 360°.”
Zakaria added that it was a dubious proposition for the U.S. to cut off trade with China over the issue of Iran.
“We’ve already seen how that would work ’cause the Chinese would cut off their exports of rare earth, and all kinds of crucial things that the United States depends on. So it seems unlikely that you’re actually gonna get at the core problem,” Zakaria said.
