sources.news_title: China Pushes Back as Trump Tightens Iran Squeeze
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, DC – August 20, 2026 (STL.News) President Donald Trump’s expanding economic campaign against Iran is putting increasing pressure on China (CHN), potentially opening another front in the already complicated relationship between Washington and Beijing as the war and confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz continue.
The latest tensions have also produced increasingly dramatic international media coverage.
Indian news outlet The Daily Jagran, for example, published a video Thursday under the headline, “Iran War Pulls In China! Xi Jinping Counters Trump’s ‘E-BOMB’ On Iran! China-US Clash Now?”
The presentation portrays CHN’s response as a direct counter to Trump’s latest pressure campaign and raises the possibility of a broader U.S.-China confrontation over Iran.
However, STL.News has not independently verified the claims, interpretations, or terminology used in The Daily Jagran video, including its reference to an “E-BOMB.”
What can be independently established is that CHN has become increasingly important to the next stage of Washington’s campaign against Tehran.
Trump turns economic pressure toward Iran’s partners
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Thursday that Washington intends to impose what he described as the toughest sanctions ever placed on Iran.
Bessent also publicly urged CHN to cooperate.
That request is significant because CHN is the dominant destination for Iranian oil shipped overseas.
According to Reuters, citing 2025 data from commodities analytics firm Kpler, China buys more than 80% of Iran’s shipped oil.
That relationship creates an obvious problem for the Trump administration.
Washington can impose increasingly severe restrictions on Iran, its banks, shipping companies and oil industry. But if Chinese buyers continue purchasing Iranian crude, Tehran retains an important source of revenue.
Bessent argued that China has its own interest in restoring stability because of its dependence on energy supplies from the Gulf.
The Treasury secretary did not publicly detail exactly what action Washington could take against Beijing if Chinese companies continue dealing with Iran, saying some discussions were better conducted privately.
China rejects sanctions as the solution
Beijing has not embraced Washington’s approach.
CHN responded Thursday by emphasizing political and diplomatic negotiations rather than additional economic pressure against Tehran.
CHN says sanctions and economic coercion will not resolve the crisis.
That leaves the world’s two largest economies approaching Iran from significantly different directions.
Trump’s administration is attempting to increase the economic cost of Iran continuing its current policies, while Beijing is publicly arguing for negotiations and opposing the use of escalating economic pressure.
China also has substantial practical reasons to resist measures that could disrupt Iranian oil.
Cheap Iranian crude has long attracted Chinese refiners, and China’s broader economy depends heavily on imported energy.
The conflict around the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz therefore presents Beijing with competing interests.
China wants to preserve its relationship with Tehran, but it also needs stability throughout the Gulf, where several of its major energy suppliers are located.
Iranian oil puts China at center of confrontation
The oil relationship is what makes China particularly important.
Iran has endured decades of U.S. sanctions, developing networks intended to keep oil moving despite restrictions on conventional international financial and shipping systems.
China has become the most important market for those exports.
That means Trump’s latest strategy could eventually force Washington to make a difficult decision: how aggressively is the United States prepared to punish Chinese companies or financial institutions involved in Iranian trade?
Secondary sanctions could increase pressure on Tehran without requiring additional military action.
But applying those measures aggressively against Chinese entities carries substantial risks.
China is not a small economy that can easily be isolated from international trade.
It is one of America’s largest trading partners and occupies strategically important positions in global manufacturing and the processing and export of critical minerals.
Reuters noted that additional economic warfare against China could provoke retaliation, including through Beijing’s leverage over strategically important rare-earth minerals.
That possibility makes the Iran confrontation potentially relevant far beyond the Middle East.
Washington expands pressure on Tehran
Trump announced Wednesday that the United States would intensify its economic campaign against Iran and warned countries, banks and companies against providing Tehran with an economic lifeline.
The administration’s strategy comes alongside existing military and maritime pressure surrounding Iran and the Strait of Hormuz.
The Treasury Department also listed new Iran-related sanctions actions Thursday as Washington continued expanding its restrictions.
Iran has rejected the administration’s threats.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi characterized Washington’s approach as economic terrorism, while Iranian officials have argued that decades of sanctions demonstrate that pressure will not force Tehran to surrender its political objectives.
The disagreement leaves little public evidence of an immediate diplomatic breakthrough.
Oil markets react to Trump’s announcement
Financial markets are already responding to the uncertainty.
Oil prices climbed sharply Thursday following Trump’s announcement.
Brent crude rose above $94 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude also advanced as traders considered whether stronger enforcement against Iranian exports could further tighten global supplies.
The implications extend well beyond Iran.
If Washington successfully reduces Iranian exports to China, Chinese refiners would need replacement supplies.
If China refuses to cooperate and Washington retaliates against Chinese companies, the consequences could expand into trade, banking, shipping and critical minerals.
And if instability around the Strait of Hormuz worsens, oil shipments from other Gulf producers could also face disruption.
That combination helps explain why an Iran policy dispute can quickly become a global economic issue.
Is China entering the Iran war?
This is where distinctions matter most.
China opposing American economic pressure does not automatically mean China has entered the Iran war militarily.
Nor does Beijing’s purchase of Iranian oil establish that Chinese forces are preparing to fight U.S. forces.
China has maintained extensive economic and diplomatic ties with Iran while simultaneously maintaining important relationships with other Middle Eastern governments.
Beijing therefore has incentives to prevent the confrontation from becoming a direct U.S.-China military crisis.
At the same time, the conflict is clearly affecting the strategic competition between Washington and Beijing.
A U.S. government commission tracking China’s involvement with Iran has documented Beijing’s continued economic relationship with Tehran and Chinese opposition to American sanctions on companies involved in Iranian oil.
China’s Ministry of Commerce previously issued a blocking order opposing certain U.S. sanctions on Chinese companies involved with Iranian oil, describing them as an improper extraterritorial application of American law.
That history demonstrates that disputes over Iranian oil and U.S. sanctions were already affecting U.S.-China relations before Trump’s latest announcement.
Viral headlines require careful distinction
The Daily Jagran presentation illustrates another dimension of the conflict: how the war is being portrayed outside the United States.
Its headline frames the situation as China being pulled into the Iran war and Xi Jinping countering Trump’s supposed “E-BOMB.”
That framing may attract attention, but readers should distinguish between a media organization’s interpretation and independently established events.
STL.News has not found independent confirmation from Reuters, U.S. government sources or other authoritative reporting establishing that the phrase “E-BOMB” represents the name of a particular U.S. weapon deployed against Iran or a formally designated policy that Xi has specifically countered.
The underlying economic confrontation, however, is real.
Trump is threatening countries and businesses that continue providing economic support to Iran.
China is Iran’s dominant overseas oil customer.
Washington wants Beijing’s cooperation.
And Beijing is publicly rejecting the idea that additional sanctions and economic pressure offer the path to resolving the conflict.
Those facts alone create significant potential for friction.
Iran could become another US-China fault line
The most important question may therefore be not whether China is “joining” the Iran war, but whether the conflict becomes another major arena for U.S.-China competition.
Washington wants to deprive Tehran of revenue.
Beijing wants to protect its economic interests, maintain access to energy, and resist American sanctions it considers extraterritorial.
Iran needs buyers for its oil.
Those interests are increasingly colliding.
For now, an important distinction remains between an economic and diplomatic confrontation and a direct military clash between China and the United States.
But the harder Washington pushes countries to sever economic ties with Iran, the more difficult that distinction could become to manage.
Editorial Note on International Video Coverage
STL.News periodically presents videos and reports from news organizations around the world to give readers an opportunity to see how journalists, commentators, and audiences in other countries perceive and discuss major international events.
The views, claims, terminology, conclusions, and editorial framing in these third-party videos belong solely to their respective publishers, presenters, and contributors. Their inclusion does not represent STL.News.
Unless specifically stated otherwise, STL.News has not independently verified the information or claims contained in these videos. Readers should treat such material as an example of international media coverage and perspective rather than as independently verified reporting by STL.News.

sources.news_title: Trump Threatens Iran Allies With ‘Tremendous’ Economic Costs
sources.text:
Highlights:
- Trump has threatened sweeping economic consequences against countries and businesses that provide Iran with financial or commercial lifelines.
- The warning comes as the US-Iran war approaches six months and tensions around the Strait of Hormuz continue to unsettle global markets.
- China, which bought more than 80 percent of Iran’s shipped oil in 2025, could face major pressure if Washington moves to cut off that trade.
- Iran says it remains open to dialogue but insists negotiations cannot amount to surrender.
- Rising oil prices and uncertainty over Middle Eastern supplies show how the conflict is already reaching beyond the battlefield.
Donald Trump is widening the pressure on Iran beyond military confrontation, warning countries, businesses and financial institutions that they could face severe economic consequences if they help keep Tehran’s economy functioning.
The warning comes as the US-Iran war approaches its six-month mark, with the conflict continuing to affect Gulf countries, global energy markets and shipping through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.
Trump’s latest message suggests that Washington’s next phase of pressure could extend well beyond Iran itself. Governments maintaining trade, financial or other economic channels with Tehran could potentially find themselves caught in the expanding confrontation.
Trump threatens economic isolation for Iran
In a social media message Wednesday, Trump promised “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.” While he did not provide detailed measures, his message made clear that Iran’s economic connections are now a central target.
“ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” Trump wrote.
The warning raises the stakes for countries that have maintained economic or diplomatic channels with Tehran, particularly as some governments have attempted to mediate between Washington and Iran.
For those countries, businesses and financial institutions, the threat creates a difficult choice: maintain connections with Iran and risk US economic pressure, or step back from Tehran as Washington seeks to isolate the country.
Why Trump’s Iran strategy matters beyond Tehran
The economic threat comes after months of fighting that has already pushed the Iran conflict far beyond a direct confrontation between Washington and Tehran.
Thousands have been killed, Gulf nations have been drawn into the crisis and global markets have been shaken by Iran’s ability to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Before the war began in February, the waterway carried about one-fifth of the world’s traded oil. Continued uncertainty over shipping through the route therefore has consequences that reach well beyond the countries directly involved in the fighting.
Two ceasefire agreements, in April and June, have already collapsed. Israel has largely withdrawn from the fighting, but the conflict has not moved toward a lasting settlement.
Trump’s latest threat adds another layer to an already volatile situation: economic pressure could now extend to countries that are not directly participating in the war.
Iran rejects pressure from Washington
Iran has faced US sanctions for decades, dating back to the 1979 Islamic Revolution. Yet Tehran has continued to resist pressure from Washington.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi accused Trump of using the confrontation to distract Americans from domestic problems, including record US debt and rising interest costs.
He said: “America’s economic terrorism threatens the global economy and the national sovereignty of countries around the world.”
Iran’s position suggests that Washington’s attempt to increase economic pressure may not produce an immediate change in Tehran’s approach.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, said Iran remains open to dialogue but does not equate negotiations with surrender. He argued that military pressure and sanctions would not break Iran’s resolve.
That leaves the confrontation at a potentially difficult stage, with both sides signaling that pressure alone may not be enough to produce a settlement.
Trump’s warning puts US allies in a difficult position
Trump’s threat could have consequences for countries attempting to maintain diplomatic or commercial relationships with Iran.
Some countries have been involved in efforts to mediate between Washington and Tehran. If those governments or their businesses face punishment for keeping economic or diplomatic channels open, the pressure campaign could broaden the conflict rather than simply isolate Iran.
The United Arab Emirates has already suspended trade activities, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran until further notice.
The move followed a UAE claim that Iran launched two missiles that fell into the sea. Tehran rejected the claim as baseless.
The UAE’s decision illustrates how regional governments are already being forced to respond to the rapidly changing economic and security environment surrounding the war.
China could become a major test for Trump’s Iran crackdown
China represents one of the biggest challenges for Trump’s economic strategy.
China bought more than 80 percent of Iran’s shipped oil in 2025, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters. Any attempt by Washington to severely restrict that trade could therefore bring the Iran conflict into closer contact with the already complicated US-China relationship.
The consequences could extend beyond energy.
China is an important part of American supply chains and is also significant to the global market for rare-earth minerals. A major confrontation over Iranian oil could therefore create additional economic pressure at a time when the relationship between Washington and Beijing already carries global implications.
For Trump, that makes enforcement of the Iran crackdown more complicated than simply targeting Tehran.
Oil prices show the economic pressure is already spreading
Markets are already reacting to uncertainty surrounding the conflict.
Oil prices climbed to three-week highs on Thursday (20) as traders worried that the standoff with Iran could continue disrupting Middle Eastern supplies.
That movement highlights why developments surrounding Iran matter to people and businesses far beyond the region. Continued disruption to energy supplies can affect markets, companies and consumers as traders attempt to assess how long the confrontation could last.
The Strait of Hormuz remains central to those concerns because of its importance to global oil shipments.
What Trump wants from Iran
Behind the economic and military pressure is a broader US objective involving Iran’s nuclear program.
Trump wants Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile and a tougher nuclear agreement to replace the deal he abandoned in 2018.
Iran, however, maintains that its nuclear program is peaceful.
The disagreement over Iran’s nuclear ambitions remains one of the central issues in the confrontation, alongside sanctions, military pressure and the continuing dispute over economic ties.
For now, Tehran is signaling that it will not simply give in under pressure, while Washington is threatening to make the economic cost of supporting Iran substantially higher.
The question now is how far the conflict spreads
Trump’s latest warning changes the potential scope of the Iran conflict. What began as a military confrontation is increasingly being felt through trade, financial relationships, energy markets and international diplomacy.
The biggest question is whether the threat of sweeping economic consequences will persuade countries and businesses to distance themselves from Tehran—or whether it will pull more governments into the dispute.
With Iran refusing to equate negotiations with surrender, oil prices responding to fears over supply disruptions and China remaining a major buyer of Iranian oil, the economic consequences of the war could extend well beyond the battlefield.
For the US, Iran and countries navigating relationships with both, the next stage may depend on whether economic pressure produces negotiations or creates another front in an already expanding conflict.

He added that Iran’s currency has become worthless and that the country is, in his words, hanging by a thread. These claims have not been independently verified, and Iranian officials have pushed back on similar assertions from Washington in the past.
Warning To Other Nations
A central part of Trump’s announcement was a direct warning to other countries. He said any nation whose financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government bodies extend any kind of lifeline to Iran would itself face tremendous economic consequences. This signals that the new campaign is designed to go beyond direct sanctions on Iran and extend pressure to its trading partners and intermediaries.
Why This Matters Now
This is a sensitive moment to make the announcement. The ceasefire between the US and Iran expired this week with the situation in the Gulf heating up. The United Arab Emirates said Iran recently fired ballistic missiles at its territory, a charge Tehran denied as a false flag. In retaliation, the UAE suspended trade and financial dealings with Iran, a major blow since the UAE was Iran’s biggest source of imports before this.
Iran is already one of the most sanctioned countries on the planet, with thousands of punitive measures aimed at its financial, energy, petrochemical, aviation and cryptocurrency sectors. Reports suggest the new US drive could target Iran’s oil trade with China, its biggest customer, and currency exchange networks in the UAE that move Iranian money around the world.
Iran’s Reaction
Iranian officials denounced the growing pressure. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has accused Washington of increasing sanctions after earlier rounds failed to force Tehran into submission, saying that this approach makes a negotiated resolution to the conflict more difficult to reach and not easier.
The Larger Context – Donald Trump Iran sanctions
Trump’s announcement doesn’t lay out specific sanctions or a formal plan of action, but it sets the stage for what could be an escalated financial siege on Iran in the weeks to come. The next few days are likely to show how far the US is willing to go, with regional tensions already high after the claims of missiles and an expired ceasefire, and how key partners such as China and the UAE will respond to the pressure being put on their dealings with Tehran.

sources.news_title: Trump now threatens Iran with ‘economic D-Day’
sources.text:
President Donald Trump is threatening a sweeping new economic campaign against Iran as the nearly six-month war continues without an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz or establish a permanent ceasefire.
Trump said Wednesday that the United States would launch what he called an “ECONOMIC D-DAY” against Iran and warned that countries, banks and businesses providing economic support to Tehran could also face U.S. penalties.
The president did not detail what additional measures the administration intends to impose beyond the extensive sanctions already in place. He said the effort would target areas including oil smuggling, financial transfers, exchange houses, ship registries and front companies.
China remains Iran’s largest trading partner, while Tehran also maintains economic ties with several Middle Eastern countries. The United Arab Emirates said Tuesday it had suspended financial and economic transactions with Iran, potentially restricting one of Tehran’s key channels for trade and access to the global financial system.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also signaled that additional measures are coming, describing them as an unprecedented attempt to economically isolate Iran and force it back to negotiations.
Trump’s warning follows the expiration Monday of a 60-day window established under a June memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran. The deadline passed without a deal on ending the war or fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which roughly 20% of the world’s oil supplies pass.
The administration has sent conflicting signals about whether negotiations continue. Senior adviser Jared Kushner said this week that backchannel talks remained active, while Iranian officials denied communications and Trump said no discussions were underway.
The White House continues to demand an end to Iran’s nuclear program as a condition for a permanent ceasefire, a requirement Tehran has so far rejected.
Source: WSJ

sources.news_title: Trump Escalates Pressure on Iran With 'Economic D-Day' Offensive
sources.text:
The United States has opened a new front in its confrontation with Iran, with President Donald Trump announcing what he called the “most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country” after declaring that Tehran had failed to seize opportunities for a diplomatic settlement.
Trump Shifts From Military Pressure to Economic Warfare
In a strongly worded statement on Truth Social, Mr Trump said Iran had “tragically” failed to reach an agreement with Washington and would now face an unprecedented campaign of economic isolation. He described the move as an “Economic D-Day” aimed at crippling Tehran’s remaining financial lifelines.
Claiming Iran’s military infrastructure has been severely weakened and its economy battered, Mr Trump said the country was “hanging by a thread” and warned that tougher measures were on the way.
Secondary Sanctions Warning to Iran’s Partners
The US president also expanded his warning beyond Iran, stating that any nation, financial institution, business, airport or government entity providing support to Tehran could face significant economic repercussions from Washington.
Trump specifically highlighted oil smuggling networks, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, swap arrangements and front companies that the US believes enable Iran to circumvent existing sanctions. The move signals an effort to tighten pressure not only on Tehran but also on countries maintaining commercial links with the Islamic Republic.
Iran Rejects Claims of Collapse
Tehran swiftly pushed back against Washington’s rhetoric.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi accused the United States of attempting to disguise what he called the failure of its military campaign by launching a new phase of economic pressure. He argued that if Iran were truly on the verge of collapse, Washington would not need to rally international support against it.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also dismissed the latest measures, calling Trump’s “Economic D-Day” announcement a diversion from America’s domestic economic challenges. He maintained that sanctions have repeatedly failed to force policy changes in Tehran.
IRGC Issues Fresh Military Warning
Adding to mounting tensions, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned that any future confrontation would involve more powerful weaponry than previously deployed.
IRGC spokesman Brig Gen Mohsen Mohebbi said Iran possesses missile warheads that are significantly more destructive than those used in earlier phases of the conflict and cautioned against further US “adventurism”.
The remarks underscore Tehran’s determination to project strength despite growing economic and diplomatic pressure.
Strait of Hormuz Remains Under Global Watch
Despite the escalating rhetoric, shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained largely unchanged, according to industry data. The waterway continues to be one of the world’s most critical energy corridors and remains central to regional security calculations.
Trump said countries were increasingly exploring alternatives to the strategic route and insisted that US measures in the region had kept maritime traffic moving. However, analysts continue to view Hormuz as a potential flashpoint capable of disrupting global energy markets.
Regional Fallout Continues
The broader conflict continues to reverberate across the Middle East.
The UAE has suspended trade, commercial exchange and financial transactions with Iran until further notice, while regional governments remain on heightened alert following recent security incidents linked to the conflict.
Meanwhile, reports of attacks on commercial shipping, Houthi threats against maritime traffic, and growing international diplomatic tensions have reinforced concerns that the crisis could further destabilise the region.
A High-Stakes Economic Offensive
Trump’s latest announcement reflects Washington’s belief that intensified financial pressure can achieve what military action and diplomacy have so far failed to deliver. Iran, however, insists it has weathered decades of sanctions and remains prepared to resist further economic coercion.
As both sides harden their positions, the effectiveness of this new economic offensive may determine the next phase of one of the Middle East’s most consequential confrontations.

sources.news_title: Trump Threatens Unprecedented Economic Warfare Against Countries Supporting Iran
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has announced a dramatic escalation in Washington’s economic campaign against Iran, warning countries and businesses that continue to provide Tehran with financial, commercial or logistical support that they could face severe economic consequences. Trump described the planned measures as an unprecedented campaign of “economic warfare and isolation,” signaling that the United States intends to increase pressure not only on Iran but also on its international trading partners.
The announcement comes as the broader conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran approaches its sixth month and diplomatic efforts remain uncertain. According to recent reports, Washington has been increasingly focused on economic pressure as an alternative to immediately expanding military operations. Trump’s latest warning therefore represents a major shift toward using financial restrictions, sanctions and international economic isolation as tools to pressure Tehran.
Trump said countries that provide Iran with what he described as a “lifeline” could face tremendous economic consequences. While he did not provide a complete list of measures, the warning could potentially include secondary sanctions targeting foreign companies, banks, shipping networks and governments that continue conducting business with Iran.
The central objective appears to be weakening Iran’s ability to generate and access foreign currency. Oil exports are particularly important because petroleum revenues represent a major source of income for Tehran. Washington has previously attempted to reduce Iranian oil exports through sanctions and enforcement actions. The latest campaign could expand those efforts by targeting the international networks that allow Iranian oil and other goods to reach global markets.
The threat could have significant consequences for countries that maintain commercial relations with Iran. China, in particular, is a major concern for Washington because it remains an important buyer of Iranian oil. Any attempt to impose aggressive secondary sanctions on Chinese companies or financial institutions could create a new confrontation between Washington and Beijing.
Other countries could also find themselves under pressure. Businesses involved in shipping, insurance, banking, energy trading and logistics could face difficult choices if Washington increases enforcement. Companies may have to decide whether maintaining Iranian business is worth risking access to the US financial system.
The situation is also closely connected to the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy routes. Disruption in the waterway has already created concerns about oil supplies and global markets. The United States has been working with partners to maintain commercial shipping, while Iran continues to exert influence over the strategic waterway.
Iran has rejected Trump’s pressure campaign. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi described the US approach as economic terrorism and argued that American threats would not force Tehran into surrender. Iran has indicated that it remains open to dialogue, but it rejects negotiations conducted under what it considers excessive pressure.
The latest US warning therefore creates a difficult diplomatic environment. Washington wants to demonstrate that Iran will face increasing costs if it refuses to compromise, while Tehran appears determined to resist what it views as coercion.
For global markets, the consequences could extend beyond the Middle East. Stricter sanctions could affect oil supplies, shipping costs, insurance premiums and international trade. If major Iranian trading partners become targets of US penalties, the dispute could also develop into a broader economic confrontation.
Trump’s announcement has consequently raised the stakes considerably. Instead of limiting economic pressure to Iranian entities, Washington is now signaling that countries helping Tehran could themselves become targets. Whether the strategy succeeds in forcing Iran back toward negotiations or instead deepens international divisions remains one of the most important questions facing the global economy and Middle Eastern diplomacy.

sources.news_title: Trump announces punitive action against Iran’s trading partners to stifle Iranian economy
sources.text:
Trump announces punitive action against Iran’s trading partners to stifle Iranian economy
text_fields
With the aim of stifling Iran economically, US President Donald Trump announced punitive action against countries that trade with or assist Iran, as the US was left with no military options to bring Iran to its knees even after a fortnight of bombardment of Iranian targets, while US military experts warned of shortages in US stockpiles of key munitions, while Iran controls the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump warned of “tremendous economic consequences” for countries, describing the consequences as the “most crushing economic operation” ever launched against any country, and said that governments, businesses and financial institutions that help Iran with an economic “lifeline” would face those consequences.
No details were provided during Trump’s announcement about the countries and punitive actions that he targeted; however, in the wake of the midterm elections in the US, and with the war nowhere near an end even after six months, pressure mounts on the administration over the lagging costs to the US economically and militarily.
The US has increasingly turned towards economic warfare after weeks of air strikes failed to bring Iran back to negotiations, as Pentagon advisers reportedly warned Trump that the US had nearly exhausted its list of viable targets in Iran and that the military campaign was approaching the limits of its effectiveness.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the US would intensify efforts to isolate Iran economically, amid the Treasury’s months-long pursuit of Operation Economic Fury, apparently targeting Iran’s revenue sources through sanctions, while ensuring that oil exports from ports in Iran be halted through a US naval blockade around the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, Iran, which has been facing Western sanctions for years, has developed its own network of intermediaries to surmount the sanctions through shell companies and shadow tankers to ensure its oil trade remains intact, while Trump demanded an end to activities including oil smuggling, cash transfers, exchange-house operations, ship registries and the use of front companies.
The threat of secondary sanctions could, however, bring the US into direct confrontation with China, Iran’s largest trading partner and principal buyer of its oil, with a warning from Gregory Brew of the Eurasia Group that any new measures would inevitably have to target Iran’s trading partners, making China the most difficult and consequential target.
The prospect is particularly sensitive as Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to visit the US next month, when the US is seeking to establish a new trading relationship with China.

sources.news_title: 'TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences': Inside Trump's Latest Secondary Sanctions Warning Over Iran
sources.text:
Washington is no longer simply threatening Iran. Donald Trump is warning the entire world to stay away from Tehran—or pay the price.
As the US-Iran war approaches its six-month mark, Trump has threatened an economic crackdown so sweeping that countries doing business with Iran could find themselves pulled directly into the conflict.
In a social media message Wednesday, Trump promised “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.” He offered few details, but the message was unmistakable: Iran’s economic lifelines are now targets, and anyone helping keep them open could become a target too.
“ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” Trump wrote.
That threat dramatically raises the stakes of a war that has already spilled far beyond the battlefield.
Trump’s Iran war goes global
Thousands have been killed, Gulf nations have been dragged into the crisis, and global markets have been rattled by Iran’s ability to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway that carried about one-fifth of the world’s traded oil before February.
Two ceasefire agreements, in April and June, have already collapsed. And while Israel has largely withdrawn from the fighting, the conflict shows little sign of settling.
Now Trump is reaching for a weapon Iran has experienced for decades: economic isolation.
Iran has lived under punishing US sanctions since the 1979 Islamic Revolution. Yet Tehran has shown little willingness to surrender under pressure.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi accused Trump of using the confrontation to distract Americans from problems at home, including record US debt and rising interest costs.
He said: “America's economic terrorism threatens the global economy and the national sovereignty of countries around the world.”
Trump’s threat is particularly explosive because it could put US allies in an impossible position. Some countries have been involved in efforts to mediate between Washington and Tehran. Punishing them for maintaining economic or diplomatic channels could widen the confrontation rather than isolate Iran.
The United Arab Emirates has already suspended trade activities, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran until further notice. The move followed a UAE claim that Iran launched two missiles that fell into the sea, a claim Tehran rejected as baseless.
China faces Trump’s economic hammer
Then there is China.
China bought more than 80 per cent of Iran’s shipped oil in 2025, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters. Any attempt to choke off that trade could turn the Iran crisis into another major US-China confrontation, especially given Beijing’s importance to American supply chains and rare-earth minerals.
And the economic pressure is already being felt. Oil prices climbed to three-week highs Thursday (20) as traders worried that the Iran standoff could continue disrupting Middle Eastern supplies.
Tehran, meanwhile, is refusing to blink.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, said Iran remains open to dialogue but does not confuse negotiations with surrender. He argued that military pressure and sanctions would not break Iran’s resolve.
That leaves Washington with a dangerous choice: escalate the economic squeeze or find a diplomatic exit.
Trump says he wants Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile and a tougher nuclear agreement to replace the deal he abandoned in 2018. Iran insists its nuclear program is peaceful.
Behind all the threats, sanctions and military pressure is one increasingly frightening question:
How far will this war spread before someone finally backs down?

sources.news_title: Trump Warns Iran Supporters of Economic Measures
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump has warned that countries providing economic or financial support to Iran could face severe consequences as Washington seeks to end the nearly six-month war involving the United States, Israel and Iran.
President Trump, in a social media post on Wednesday, threatened “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale,” warning that countries allowing their financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities to provide “any type of lifeline to Iran” would face “TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences.”
The conflict has killed thousands and disrupted global markets, with Iran demonstrating its ability to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route that previously carried about one-fifth of globally traded oil.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi accused Trump of trying to divert attention from U.S. economic challenges, including record debt and rising interest rates.
“America’s economic terrorism threatens the global economy and the national sovereignty of countries around the world,” Araqchi said on X.
US President did not specify what measures Washington would impose, while his threats could potentially affect U.S. allies involved in peace efforts. The United Arab Emirates, which hosts a major U.S. military base, has meanwhile suspended trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran until further notice.
China remains Iran’s largest oil buyer, purchasing more than 80% of its shipped crude in 2025, according to Kpler data. However, tougher U.S. measures against China could risk retaliation given Beijing’s importance as a supplier of critical goods, including rare earth minerals.

sources.news_title: Trump Watch: Trump threatens countries that keep doing business with Iran
sources.text:
Donald Trump matters a lot to Mzansi and the rest of the world right now. Trump is changing the way America works – and how the world’s most powerful country deals with the rest of the world.
We’ll track what he does and connect the dots to your daily life.
Trump threatens countries that keep doing business with Iran
US President Donald Trump has announced a new plan to put more economic pressure on Iran.
Trump said any country that helps Iran or does business with it could face major economic punishment from the US.
He said this could include countries whose banks, businesses, airports or government bodies help Iran.
Trump did not explain exactly what punishment would be used or which countries could be targeted.
The US has already placed many sanctions on Iran and is trying to stop the country from selling oil.
Trump also said activities such as oil smuggling, cash transfers and the use of fake companies must stop.
The move could create new tension with China, which is Iran’s biggest trading partner and buys Iranian oil.
Iran said sanctions and military pressure would not force it to give in, but said it was still open to talks with the US.
Image source: @WhiteHouse
Trump says Iran talks are off
US President Donald Trump says there are no talks planned with Iran and that a US naval blockade remains in place.
Trump also said the Strait of Hormuz was open and operating, and that all sea mines had been removed or destroyed.
Iran disagreed. A senior Iranian official said the strait would stay closed until the US followed the terms of an agreement signed in June.
Iran wants the US to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, remove oil sanctions, release frozen Iranian money and stop military attacks and threats.
Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner had said a day earlier that talks between the US and Iran were still happening.
Trump then said there were no talks taking place and none had been scheduled.
Attempts to reach a peace deal have now stalled. The war began when the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February.
A senior Iranian official said Iran could now move to a more aggressive military approach because talks had failed.
Image source: File
Trump tells rescued boy he probably would not have saved him
US President Donald Trump has told a 10-year-old boy who nearly drowned that he probably would not have saved him.
Trump made the comment while honouring 16-year-old lifeguard Ryder Williams at the White House.
Ryder rescued Nathaniel Rai after the boy was swept into deep water at a beach in California last month.
Video showed Ryder swimming into rough waves, grabbing Nathaniel and fighting his way back to shore.
Trump praised Ryder as a hero and said he would receive a high civilian honour.
But Trump then joked that Nathaniel was lucky he had not been the lifeguard that day.
“I don’t know if I’d do it. I wouldn’t, probably,” Trump said.
Ryder said he relied on his training during the rescue and hoped people would try to help others whenever they could.
Image source: File
Trump cuts South Korea drills after praising Kim Jong Un
US President Donald Trump says the US will reduce military exercises with South Korea.
Trump said the drills cost too much and sent the wrong message to North Korea.
He also pointed to his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
The US and South Korea were due to start their yearly military exercises on Monday. Trump said it was too late to cancel them completely, but future drills would be reduced.
Trump also criticised South Korea for refusing to join the US in its efforts against Iran’s nuclear programme.
South Korea said it was looking at Trump’s comments. It said it hoped his relationship with Kim could help bring North Korea back to talks.
Trump’s decision comes after North Korea carried out new missile tests this month. The United Nations has banned North Korea from carrying out these tests.
Trump has cut military exercises with South Korea before. In 2018, he stopped them during talks with Kim and said the drills were too expensive.
Image source: File
Trump plans to give electric shock gloves to immigration officers
Donald Trump’s government plans to spend up to $20-million on electric shock gloves for US immigration officers.
The Department of Homeland Security says it could buy the gloves by March next year. They would be given to officers working for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as ICE.
The gloves can send electric shocks through a person’s skin. The company that makes them says the shocks are meant to distract someone and make it harder for them to move.
The gloves can produce up to 380 volts. The government says they would be used to help officers control difficult situations.
The plan has angered human rights groups. They fear the gloves could be used against immigrants and protesters.
ICE has already faced criticism over the way some officers have treated people. Critics have accused agents of using too much force and unfairly targeting people because of their race.
The company that makes the gloves says they are safe and do not cause injury. It also says they should not be used on some people, including small children, pregnant women and elderly people.
The planned deal could be worth between $10-million and $20-million.
Image source: File
Trump sued over paid early access to social media posts
US President Donald Trump has been sued over a paid service that gives some people early access to his Truth Social posts.
The service, called Truth API, charges up to $100,000 a month.
It gives paying customers faster access to posts from Trump and other senior US officials, including Vice President JD Vance and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt.
The lawsuit was filed by the Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation. They say the service is unfair and could allow Trump to profit from information he shares as president.
Trump has used Truth Social to announce major news about tariffs and the war with Iran. Some of those posts have moved stock and oil prices.
Trump Media says the service gives businesses quick access to posts that can move markets. The company said it already had more than 10 customers.
The lawsuit says Trump could personally benefit because he is the largest shareholder in Trump Media.
The groups want a court to stop the White House from using Truth Social as the only place for official announcements while some people pay to see them first.
Image source: File
Trump confirms secret plane switch after Iran threat
US President Donald Trump has confirmed that he secretly changed planes after leaving a Nato summit in Turkey last month because of a possible threat.
Trump said the Secret Service and the military told him to use a different plane. He said he followed their instructions.
Reports said Trump first boarded Air Force One in front of cameras on 8 July. He was then secretly moved off the plane in a catering truck and taken to a smaller military aircraft.
US officials said there was a real threat from Iran that a missile could be fired at Trump’s plane. One report said a person near the summit had been seen with a shoulder-fired missile.
Journalists and some White House staff stayed on the original plane and did not know Trump had left. They were told to keep the window shades closed.
Trump said the smaller plane may also have been in danger because attackers could have expected him to use it instead.
The secret plane flew Trump to Britain, where he later moved back onto the older Air Force One before being seen by reporters again.
Trump said he receives many threats and has previously said Iran sees him as its main target.
Image source: File
Trump used secret flight after Iran assassination threat
US President Donald Trump was secretly moved onto a smaller military plane during a trip from Turkey to Britain last month.
The move was reportedly made because of a serious threat from Iran to assassinate him.
Trump first boarded an older Air Force One in front of cameras after a Nato summit in Ankara.
But minutes later, he was secretly taken off the plane and moved in an airport catering truck. He was then put onto a smaller US Air Force plane.
Reporters and even some White House staff believed Trump was still on the old Air Force One.
The smaller plane flew Trump to Britain. The old Air Force One followed and arrived only minutes later.
Trump was then moved back onto the older plane before stepping out in front of cameras, making it look as if he had travelled on it the whole way.
The White House said it uses every tool available to protect Trump because there are people who want to harm him.
Image source: File
Israel rejects Trump Gaza peace plan
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected Donald Trump’s 15 point peace plan for Gaza.
Netanyahu said Israeli troops would not leave Gaza until Hamas had fully given up its weapons.
Trump’s peace team said last month that Hamas had agreed to disarm. Hamas said it would only hand over its heavy weapons if Israel stopped its attacks and pulled its forces out.
Netanyahu said Israel would not accept the plan as it stands. He said Hamas had to disarm properly before any Israeli withdrawal.
Hamas said it was still committed to the agreement and was ready to help carry it out.
Trump’s plan includes Hamas giving up its weapons, Israeli troops leaving Gaza and rebuilding the area.
A senior official working on Trump’s plan said talks were still happening. He said the plan remained the best way forward.
Netanyahu said he was still speaking to US officials about what happens next, but made clear that Israel did not agree with all parts of Trump’s plan.
Image source: File
Trump denies US is running low on weapons
US President Donald Trump has denied reports that America is running short of weapons during the war with Iran.
Trump said the US has “massive amounts” of weapons and that more are being made and sent where needed.
His government is facing growing questions about how many missiles are left after months of fighting.
Reports say the US has used large amounts of long-range missiles and other weapons since the war began.
Trump also threatened long jail sentences for people he believes leaked information about possible shortages.
He called the reports false and said Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was doing a good job.
Iran said the reports showed that US military supplies were becoming weaker. Its defence minister said Iran could still respond to any threat.
The exact number of US missiles is secret. But one research group estimated that America may have used a large part of some of its missile supply.
Image source: File
Trump says Iran deal is close
US President Donald Trump says a deal with Iran may be close, even though Iran says it is not holding talks with the US.
Trump said discussions were happening whether Iran admitted it or not. Iran rejected that claim.
Iran’s deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibadadi said talks were only taking place with Oman.
He said the US was ready to return to earlier promises. He did not explain exactly what those promises were.
The US and Iran signed a temporary agreement in June. Iran was meant to allow ships through the Strait of Hormuz without charge for 60 days.
In return, the US agreed to lift its naval blockade of Iranian ships.
Iran says a new agreement with Oman about the strait is close. It wants shipping routes changed because it says the old routes are no longer safe.
US officials have also said a deal to reopen the strait could be reached soon. Reports of explosions near ships off Yemen and Oman were still being investigated.
Image source: File
Armed man arrested at Trump golf club before visit
A man carrying a loaded gun has been arrested at Donald Trump’s golf club near Los Angeles.
Police said the arrest happened on Sunday, two days before Trump was due to visit the club for a Republican fundraising dinner.
The man was identified as 38-year-old Jeanine John Taele. Police said he had been taking photos and videos of the golf course while watching security preparations.
Officers found a loaded magazine in his pocket. They later found a loaded pistol and another magazine in his car.
Police also searched his home with the FBI. They said they found an illegally changed rifle, another pistol, body armour and large amounts of ammunition.
Officers also found radio equipment and notebooks with what they called worrying statements.
Police said they had not found any clear threat to the public. Taele is being held without bail while prosecutors decide what charges he may face.
Trump’s visit forms part of a campaign trip through California and Nevada before the November elections.
Image source: File
Trump gives Iran final warning before more attacks
US President Donald Trump says talks with Iran are still happening, even though Iran says they are not.
Trump said he agreed to keep talking after requests from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and other countries.
He called it Iran’s last chance to sign a deal before facing what he described as “decapitation”.
Trump said the talks were about reopening the Strait of Hormuz and stopping Iran from developing nuclear weapons.
He said the strait could reopen as soon as tomorrow. But he said a nuclear deal could take longer.
